claim: When choosing between options, such as food items presented in plain view, people tend to choose the option they spend longer looking at.
source: When choosing between options, such as food items presented in plain view, people tend to choose the option they spend longer looking at.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract, setting up the context for the study.

claim: The prevailing interpretation is that visual attention increases value.
source: The prevailing interpretation is that visual attention increases value.
evidence: This describes the current dominant view in the field, which the study aims to challenge.

claim: In previous studies, 'value' was coupled to a behavioural goal, since subjects had to choose the item they preferred.
source: However, in previous studies, 'value' was coupled to a behavioural goal, since subjects had to choose the item they preferred.
evidence: This is a characterization of previous research designs.

claim: Attention does not boost value, but instead it modulates goal-relevant information.
source: Combining psychophysics with computational modelling, we show that, contrary to the current interpretation, attention does not boost value, but instead it modulates goal-relevant information.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data and computational modeling.

claim: People tend to look for longer at the options with higher values.
source: In this context, robust empirical evidence has shown that people tend to look for longer at the options with higher values (Anderson et al., 2011; Gluth et al., 2018; Gluth et al., 2020) and that they tend to choose the option they pay more visual attention to (Krajbich et al., 2010; Krajbich and Rangel, 2011; Folke et al., 2017; Cavanagh et al., 2014; Thomas et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: People tend to choose the option they pay more visual attention to.
source: In this context, robust empirical evidence has shown that people tend to look for longer at the options with higher values (Anderson et al., 2011; Gluth et al., 2018; Gluth et al., 2020) and that they tend to choose the option they pay more visual attention to (Krajbich et al., 2010; Krajbich and Rangel, 2011; Folke et al., 2017; Cavanagh et al., 2014; Thomas et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The most common interpretation is that attention is allocated to items based on their value and that looking or attending to an option boosts its value.
source: The most common interpretation is that attention is allocated to items based on their value and that looking or attending to an option boosts its value, either by amplifying it (Krajbich et al., 2010; Krajbich and Rangel, 2011; Smith and Krajbich, 2019) or by shifting it upwards by a constant amount (Cavanagh et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the prevailing theoretical interpretation in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The attentional drift diffusion model (aDDM) considers that visual attention boosts the drift rate of the stochastic accumulation processes.
source: This intuition has been elegantly formalised using models of sequential sampling, in particular the attentional drift diffusion model (aDDM), which considers that visual attention boosts the drift rate of the stochastic accumulation processes (Krajbich et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes a specific computational model from previous research.

claim: The aDDM has been used to study the role of attention in the accumulation of perceptual information.
source: More recently, this same model has been also used to study the role of attention in the accumulation of perceptual information (Tavares et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The predominant assumption in the field of neuroeconomics has become that attention operates over the value of the alternatives.
source: As consequence of this development, the predominant assumption in the field of neuroeconomics has become that attention operates over the value of the alternatives (Smith and Krajbich, 2019).
evidence: This describes the current dominant view in neuroeconomics, supported by a citation.

claim: Some recent studies have called into question the assumption that attention operates over value and have hinted towards a flexible role of attention on sampling goal-relevant options.
source: However, some recent studies have called into question this assumption and have hinted towards a flexible role of attention on sampling goal-relevant options (Kovach et al., 2014; Glickman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent research that challenges the dominant view.

claim: Recent developments have shown that the 'value networks' in the brain could be tracking not purely reward value, but actually goal-congruent information.
source: Even further, recent developments have shown that the 'value networks' in the brain could be tracking not purely reward value, but actually goal-congruent information (Frömer et al., 2019; Suri et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent neuroscience research.

claim: In the like frame, participants looked for longer at the item they were about to choose – the item they deemed most valuable.
source: To anticipate our results, in the like frame condition we replicated the typical gaze-boosting effect: participants looked for longer at the item they were about to choose – the item they deemed most valuable.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from the study.

claim: In the dislike frame, participants looked for longer at the item that they then chose to eliminate, that is, the least valuable item.
source: In the dislike frame, however, participants looked for longer at the item that they then chose to eliminate, that is, the least valuable item.
evidence: This is a key experimental finding from the study.

claim: Participants paid more attention to the option they selected in the task, not to the option to which they deemed more valuable or wanted to consume.
source: This means that agents paid more attention to the option they selected in the task, not to the option to which they deemed more valuable or wanted to consume.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Participants confirmed that they understood the task and chose higher value items in the like frame and lower value items in the dislike frame.
source: Our results confirmed that participants understood the task and chose higher value items in the like frame and lower value items in the dislike frame (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: The effect of value on choice was modulated by confidence.
source: This effect was modulated by confidence (Figure 1B) similarly to previous studies (De Martino et al., 2013; Folke et al., 2017; Boldt et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and citations to previous studies.

claim: Participants preferentially gaze the higher value option during like frame.
source: Our data strongly supported the second hypothesis because we found participants preferentially gaze (Figure 2A) the higher value option during like (t(30) = 7.56, p<0.001) and the lower value option during dislike frame (t(30) = -4.99, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Participants preferentially gaze the lower value option during dislike frame.
source: Our data strongly supported the second hypothesis because we found participants preferentially gaze (Figure 2A) the higher value option during like (t(30) = 7.56, p<0.001) and the lower value option during dislike frame (t(30) = -4.99, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The difference between the time participants spent observing the right over left item (ΔDT) was a positive predictor of choice both in like and dislike frames.
source: From a hierarchical logistic regression analysis predicting choice (Figure 2B), the difference between the time participants spent observing the right over left item (ΔDT) was a positive predictor of choice both in like (z = 6.448, p<0.001) and dislike (z = 6.750, p<0.001) frames.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Participants looked for longer at the item that better fits the frame and not at the item with the highest value.
source: This means that participants looked for longer at the item that better fits the frame and not at the item with the highest value.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The magnitude of the effect of ΔDT on choice was slightly lower in the dislike case.
source: Notably, the magnitude of this effect was slightly lower in the dislike case (t(30) = 2.31, p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In the Perceptual Experiment, participants' gaze was preferentially allocated to the relevant option in each frame.
source: Critically for our main hypothesis, we found that participants' gaze was preferentially allocated to the relevant option in each frame (Figure 2C): they spent more time observing the circle with more dots during most frame (t(31)=13.85, p<0.001) and the one with less dots during fewest frame (t(31)=-10.88, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In the Perceptual Experiment, ΔDT was a positive predictor of choice in most and fewest frames.
source: ΔDT was a positive predictor of choice (Figure 2D) in most (z = 10.249, p<0.001), and fewest (z = 10.449, p<0.001) frames.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In the Perceptual Study, the effect of ΔDT on choice was higher in the fewest frame compared to the most frame.
source: Contrary to the results in the Value Experiment in which the effect of ΔDT on choice was slightly more marked in the like condition (Figure 2B), in the Perceptual Study the effect of ΔDT was the opposite: ΔDT had a higher effect in the fewest frame (ΔDTMost-Few: t(31)=-2.17, p<0.05)(Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis comparing the two frames.

claim: An important prediction of attentional accumulation models is that the chosen item is generally fixated last.
source: An important prediction of attentional accumulation models is that the chosen item is generally fixated last (unless that item is much worse than the other alternative), with the magnitude of this effect related to the difference in value between the alternatives.
evidence: This describes a theoretical prediction from computational models.

claim: The last fixation effect has been consistently replicated in various previous studies.
source: This feature of the decision has been consistently replicated in various previous studies (Krajbich et al., 2010; Krajbich and Rangel, 2011; Krajbich et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In the Value Experiment, in both frames, the last fixation effect and its modulation by value difference between the last fixated option and the other one was replicated.
source: In the Value Experiment in both frames, we replicated the last fixation effect and its modulation by value difference between the last fixated option and the other one (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In the like frame, the probability of choosing the last item fixated upon increases when the value of the last item is higher.
source: In the like frame, the probability of choosing the last item fixated upon increases when the value of the last item is higher, as is shown by the positive sign of the slope of the logistic curve (mean βLike = 0.922).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: During the dislike frame, the probability of choosing the last seen option increases when the value of the non-chosen item is higher.
source: Crucially, during the dislike frame the opposite effect was found: the probability of choosing the last seen option increases when the value of the non-chosen item is higher, seen from the negative slope of the curve (mean βDislike = −0.951; ΔβLike-Dislike: t(30)=7.963, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In the Perceptual Experiment, in the most frame, it was more probable that the last fixation was on the chosen item when the fixated circle had a higher number of dots.
source: In the most frame, it was more probable that the last fixation was on the chosen item when the fixated circle had a higher number of dots (mean βMost = 1.581).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In the Perceptual Experiment, in the fewest frame, it was more likely that the last circle seen was chosen when it had fewer dots.
source: In the fewest frame, the effect flipped: it was more likely that the last circle seen was chosen when it had fewer dots (mean βFew = −0.944; ΔβMost-Few: t(31)=3.727, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: After removing the last two fixations when calculating the ΔDT, the pattern of results is unchanged.
source: In Appendix 2—figure 3, we show that once removed the last two fixations the pattern of results is unchanged.
evidence: This is supported by additional analysis presented in the appendix.

claim: Middle fixations duration increases when the difference in value ratings of the fixated minus unfixated item increases in like and most frames.
source: Previous studies (Krajbich et al., 2010; Krajbich and Rangel, 2011; Tavares et al., 2017) have reported that middle fixations duration increases when the difference in value ratings (or perceptual evidence) of the fixated minus unfixated item increases. We replicated this result for our like and most frames but critically the effect was reversed in dislike and fewest frames (i.e. middle fixations durations decreased when the relative value of the fixated item was higher).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and comparison with previous studies.

claim: The effect on middle fixations duration was reversed in dislike and fewest frames.
source: We replicated this result for our like and most frames but critically the effect was reversed in dislike and fewest frames (i.e. middle fixations durations decreased when the relative value of the fixated item was higher).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: After an initial phase in which there was no clear gaze preference for any of the items, fixations were correlated with the frame-relevant item.
source: We observed that after an initial phase in which there was no clear gaze preference for any of the items (note that given the gaze-contingent design participants must explore both alternatives), fixations were correlated with the frame-relevant item: during like frame, fixations positions were positively correlated with ΔValue, that is the fixations were directed towards the item with higher value; during dislike frame the behaviour was the opposite: fixations were negatively correlated with ΔValue, indicating a preference for the option with lower value.
evidence: This is supported by time-series analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The magnitude of ΔValue (|ΔValue|) had a positive influence on confidence in like and dislike frames.
source: We found that the magnitude of ΔValue (|ΔValue|) had a positive influence on confidence in like (z = 5.465, p<0.001) and dislike (z = 6.300, p<0.001) frames, indicating that participants reported higher confidence when the items have a larger difference in value; this effect was larger in the dislike frame (t(30) = -4.72, p<0.01).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Reaction time (RT) had a negative effect on confidence in like and dislike frames.
source: Reaction time (RT) had a negative effect on confidence in like (z = −6.373, p<0.001) and dislike (z = −7.739, p<0.001) frames, that is, confidence was lower when the RTs were longer.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Higher number of gaze switches (gaze shift frequency, GSF) predicted lower values of confidence in like and dislike frames.
source: Additionally, we found that, in both conditions, higher number of gaze switches (i.e. gaze shift frequency, GSF) predicted lower values of confidence in like (z = −2.365, p<0.05) and dislike (z = −2.589, p<0.05) frames, as reported in Folke et al., 2017.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and citation to previous work.

claim: ΣValue had a positive effect on confidence in the like frame.
source: As in Folke et al., 2017, we found a positive effect of ΣValue on confidence in the like frame (z = 3.206, p<0.01); that is, participants reported a higher confidence level when both options were high in value.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and citation to previous work.

claim: The effect of ΣValue on confidence was inverted in the dislike frame.
source: Interestingly, this effect was inverted in the dislike frame (z = −4.492, p<0.001), with a significant difference between the two frames (t(30)=9.91, p<0.001) This means that, contrary to what happened in the like frame in which confidence was boosted when both items had high value, in the dislike frame confidence increased when both items had low value.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The change in context generates a reassessment of the evidence used to generate the confidence reports.
source: This novel finding reveals that the change in context also generates a reassessment of the evidence used to generate the confidence reports; that is, confidence also tracks goal-relevant information.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings about confidence.

claim: In the Perceptual Experiment, |ΔDots| had a positive influence on confidence in most and fewest frames.
source: Specifically, we found that |ΔDots| had a positive influence on confidence in most (z = 3.546, p<0.001) and fewest frames (z = 7.571, p<0.001), indicating that participants reported higher confidence when the evidence was stronger.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The effect of absolute evidence |ΔDots| on confidence was bigger in the fewest frame.
source: The effect of absolute evidence |ΔDots| on confidence was bigger in the fewest frame (t(31)=-4.716, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In the Perceptual Experiment, RT had a negative effect over confidence in most and fewest frames.
source: RT had a negative effect over confidence in most (z = −7.599, p<0.001) and fewest frames (z = −5.51, p<0.001), that is, faster trials were associated with higher confidence.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In the Perceptual Experiment, GSF predicted lower values of confidence in most and fewest frames.
source: We also found that GSF predicted lower values of confidence in most (z = −4.354, p<0.001) and fewest (z = −5.204, p<0.001) frames.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In the Perceptual Experiment, the effect of the sum of evidence (ΣDots) on confidence changes sign depending on the frame.
source: Critically (like in the Value Experiment), the effect of the sum of evidence (ΣDots) on confidence also changes sign depending on the frame. While ΣDots had a positive effect over confidence in the most frame (z = 2.061, p<0.05), this effect is the opposite in the fewest frame (z = −7.135, p<0.001), with a significant difference between the parameters in both frames (t(31)=14.621, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The GLAM belongs to the family of race models and approximates the aDDM model.
source: The GLAM belongs to the family of race models and approximates the aDDM model (Krajbich et al., 2010; Krajbich and Rangel, 2011) in which the dynamic aspect is discarded, favouring a more efficient estimation of the parameters.
evidence: This describes the computational model used in the study.

claim: The GLAM allows testing the prediction of the confidence measures as balance of evidence.
source: This model was chosen since, unlike the aDDM, it allowed us to test the prediction of the confidence measures as balance of evidence (Vickers, 1979; Kepecs et al., 2008; De Martino et al., 2013).
evidence: This explains the rationale for choosing GLAM over aDDM.

claim: In both experiments, goal-relevant evidence (not the value or the number of dots) was used to fit the models in the dislike and fewest frames.
source: Crucially, in both experiments, we used goal-relevant evidence (not the value or the number of dots) to fit the models in the dislike and fewest frames (for further details see the Materials and methods Attentional Model: Glam section).
evidence: This describes a key methodological choice in the modeling approach.

claim: In the Value Experiment, the model replicated the observed decrease of RT when |ΔValue| is high.
source: In both like and dislike frames, the model replicated the observed decrease of RT when |ΔValue| is high, that is, the increase in speed of response in easier trials (bigger value difference).
evidence: This is supported by model simulations compared to experimental data.

claim: In the Value Experiment, the RT simulated by the models significantly correlated with the RT values observed in participants odd-numbered trials.
source: The RT simulated by the models significantly correlated with the RT values observed in participants odd-numbered trials (Like: r(29)=0.90, p<0.001; Dislike: r(29)=0.89, p<0.001) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis comparing model predictions to data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In the Value Experiment, the model correctly predicted a higher probability of choosing the right item when ΔValue is higher in the like frame.
source: In the like frame, the model also correctly predicted a higher probability of choosing the right item when ΔValue is higher.
evidence: This is supported by model simulations compared to experimental data.

claim: In the Value Experiment, in the dislike frame, the model captured the change in the task goal and predicted that the selection of the right item will occur when -ΔValue is higher.
source: In the dislike frame, the model captured the change in the task goal and predicted that the selection of the right item will occur when -ΔValue is higher, that is when the value of the left item is higher.
evidence: This is supported by model simulations compared to experimental data.

claim: In the Value Experiment, the observed and predicted probabilities of choosing the most valuable item were significantly correlated in both frames.
source: Overall, in both frames the observed and predicted probabilities of choosing the most valuable item were significantly correlated (Like: r(29)=0.80, p<0.001; Dislike: r(29)=0.79, p<0.001) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis comparing model predictions to data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In the Value Experiment, the models predicted choice depending on the difference in gaze (ΔGaze) in both frames.
source: In both frames, the models also predicted choice depending on the difference in gaze (ΔGaze = gright – gleft), that is, that the probability of choosing the right item increases when the time spent observing that item is higher.
evidence: This is supported by model simulations.

claim: In the Value Experiment, most of the participants had a positive gaze influence and it was properly predicted by the model in both frames.
source: As in Thomas et al., 2019, most of the participants had a positive gaze influence and it was properly predicted by the model in both frames (Like: r(29)=0.68, p<0.001; Dislike: r(29)=0.63, p<0.001) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis comparing model predictions to data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In the Perceptual Experiment, the model simulations replicated the relationship between RT and |ΔDots|.
source: We replicated the relationship between RT and |ΔDots| (Most: r(26)=0.97, p<0.001; Fewest: r(26)=0.98, p<0.001) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis comparing model predictions to data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In the Perceptual Experiment, the model predicted a higher probability of choosing the right-hand item when ΔDots is higher in the most frame and when -ΔDots is higher in the fewest frame.
source: As in the value-based experiment, the model also predicted a higher probability of choosing the right-hand item when ΔDots is higher in the most frame and when -ΔDots is higher in the fewest frame.
evidence: This is supported by model simulations compared to experimental data.

claim: In the Perceptual Experiment, the simulated choices only in the fewest frame were significantly correlated with the observed data.
source: However, in the Perceptual Experiment, the simulated choices only in the fewest frame were significantly correlated with the observed data, although we observed a non-significant trend in the most frame (Most: r(26)=0.69, p<0.001; Fewest: r(26)=0.37, p=0.051) (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis comparing model predictions to data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In the Perceptual Experiment, the model predicted that choice was linked to ΔGaze in both frames.
source: In both frames, we observed that the model predicted that choice was linked to ΔGaze and, as in the Value Experiment, we show that the gaze influence predicted by the model is indeed observed in the data (Most: r(26)=0.65, p<0.001; Fewest: r(26)=0.47, p<0.05) (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis comparing model predictions to data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Models fitted without accounting for the change in goal-relevant evidence provided a poor fit of the data.
source: Results of the models fitted without accounting for the change in goal-relevant evidence provided a poor fit of the data, these results are presented in Appendix 5—figures 1–3 and 6.
evidence: This is supported by model comparison analysis presented in the appendix.

claim: For dislike and fewest frames, the best aDDM model was the one fitted using goal-relevant evidence.
source: Additionally, we were able to mirror the results obtained with GLAM using aDDM (Krajbich et al., 2010; Tavares et al., 2017). For dislike and fewest frames, the best model was the one fitted using goal-relevant evidence (see Appendix 7 for details).
evidence: This is supported by model comparison analysis presented in the appendix.

claim: Balance of evidence is defined as the absolute difference between the accumulators for each option at the moment of choice.
source: Balance of evidence is defined as the absolute difference between the accumulators for each option at the moment of choice, which is when one of them reaches the decision threshold (i.e., Δe = |Eright(tfinal) - Eleft(tfinal)|) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This defines a computational measure used in the modeling.

claim: In the Value Experiment, the model replicated the pattern of results obtained experimentally for confidence.
source: We found that this model replicated the pattern of results we obtained experimentally (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by comparing model simulations to experimental data.

claim: In the Value Experiment, ΣValue boosted Δe in the like frame and reduced Δe in the dislike frame.
source: As we have shown when analysing confidence, ΣValue boosted Δe in the like frame (βΣValue = 0.071, t(37196) = 14.21, p<0.001) and reduced Δe in the dislike frame (βΣValue = −0.061, t(37196) = −12.07, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of model simulations.

claim: In the Value Experiment, the replication of the effect for ΣValue over Δe with GLAM did not hold when the gaze bias was taken out of the model.
source: Interestingly, the replication of the effect for ΣValue over Δe with GLAM did not hold when the gaze bias was taken out of the model in like (βΣValue = −0.007, t(37196) = −1.495, p=0.13, ns) and dislike (βΣValue = −0.002, t(37196) = −0.413, p=0.679, ns) frames (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of model simulations shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In the Perceptual Experiment, ΣDots boosted Δe in the most frame and reduced Δe in the fewest frame.
source: We found that ΣDots boosted Δe in the most frame (Most : βΣDots = 0.029, t(33596) = 4.71, p<0.001) and reduced Δe in the fewest frame (Fewest : βΣDots = −0.088, t(33596) = −14.41, p<0.001) .
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of model simulations.

claim: In the Perceptual Experiment, the effect of ΣDots on Δe disappeared when the gaze bias was taken out of the model.
source: As in the Value Experiment, this effect disappeared when the gaze bias was taken out of the model (Most: βΣDots = −0.0002, t(33596) = −0.04, p=0.96, ns; Fewest: βΣDots = −0.006, t(33596) = −1.03, p=0.29, ns) (see Appendix 8—figure 2 and Appendix 8—figure 3B,E for more details).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of model simulations.

claim: The model is capable of capturing the novel empirical effect on confidence identified experimentally.
source: Overall, these results show how the model is capable of capturing the novel empirical effect on confidence we identified experimentally, giving computational support to the hypothesis that goal-relevant evidence is fed to second order processes like confidence.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modeling results.

claim: Asymmetries in the accumulation process, in particular the multiplicative effect of attention over accumulation of evidence, may enhance the differences between items that are more relevant for the frame.
source: It also hints at a potential origin to the effects of the sum of evidence (i.e. ΣValue, ΣDots) on confidence: asymmetries in the accumulation process, in particular the multiplicative effect of attention over accumulation of evidence, may enhance the differences between items that are more relevant for the frame.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the mechanism underlying the observed effects.

claim: When one has to choose the best item, it is more useful to acquire information that is likely to change the ranking at the top than information that changes the ranking at the bottom.
source: The intuition behind both results is that when one has to choose the best item, it is more useful to acquire information that is likely to change the ranking at the top (i.e. between best or second best item) than information that changes the ranking at the bottom, since these items won't be selected (e.g. 4th and 5th item).
evidence: This is an explanation of the intuition behind the economic model.

claim: The reverse is true when one is tasked to select which item to eliminate.
source: Crucially, the reverse is true when one is tasked to select which item to eliminate.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the economic model.

claim: In many ecological settings, in which there are more than two options, the optimal strategy involves acquiring asymmetric information depending on the goal.
source: Our model suggests that in many ecological settings, in which there are more than two options, the optimal strategy involves acquiring asymmetric information depending on the goal.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the economic model.

claim: It is only when there are only two options that individuals are indifferent about which information to acquire.
source: It is only when there are only two options that individuals are indifferent about which information to acquire.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the economic model.

claim: The results favour the hypothesis that attention is allocated depending on the behavioural goal of the task in both perceptual and value-based tasks.
source: Our results favour the second hypothesis: specifically, we show that, in both perceptual and value-based tasks, attention is allocated depending on the behavioural goal of the task.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on experimental data.

claim: The findings speak in favour of a more general role played by attention in prioritising the information needed to fulfil a behavioural goal in both value and perceptual choices.
source: Our findings speak in favour of a more general role played by attention in prioritising the information needed to fulfil a behavioural goal in both value and perceptual choices (Gottlieb, 2012; Kovach et al., 2014; Glickman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study supported by citations to related work.

claim: The seeking of goal-relevant information is observed along the trial, opposing the assumption that attentional sampling is random except for the last fixation.
source: Importantly, the seeking of goal-relevant information is observed along the trial, opposing the assumption that attentional sampling is random except for the last fixation (Krajbich et al., 2010; Krajbich and Rangel, 2011; see Gluth et al., 2018; Gluth et al., 2020 for additional support for this idea).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study supported by citations.

claim: The fact that almost identical results were found in a follow-up perceptual study suggests that attention acts on a more fundamental mechanism of information processing that goes beyond simple Pavlovian influences.
source: However, the fact that we found almost identical results in a follow-up perceptual study in which the choice was not framed in terms of 'accept' or 'reject' but using a different kind of instruction (i.e. 'choose the option with fewer or more dots') suggests that attention acts on a more fundamental mechanism of information processing that goes beyond simple Pavlovian influences.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing results across the two experiments.

claim: Confidence is influenced by the perceived sense of uncertainty in the evaluation process and contextual cues.
source: We found that the role of confidence goes beyond that of simply tracking the probability of an action being correct, as proposed in standard signal detection theory. Instead, it is also influenced by the perceived sense of uncertainty in the evaluation process (Navajas et al., 2017; Vaghi et al., 2017), and contextual cues (Lebreton et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental findings and citations to related work.

claim: Confidence influences future responses and information seeking.
source: In turn, confidence influences future responses and information seeking (Folke et al., 2017; Guggenmos et al., 2016; Fleming et al., 2018; Rollwage et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The sense of confidence is shaped by the behavioural goal that participants are set to achieve.
source: This suggests that similarly to attention, the sense of confidence is also shaped by the behavioural goal that participants are set to achieve.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings about confidence.

claim: The incorporation of goal-relevant evidence to fit the GLAM resulted in a better model fit compared with the model in which the value or perceptual evidence was integrated independently of the frame.
source: In both experiments, the incorporation of goal-relevant evidence to fit the GLAM resulted in a better model fit compared with the model in which the value or perceptual evidence was integrated independently of the frame.
evidence: This is supported by model comparison analysis.

claim: The empirical confidence data provide support to a multiplicative instead of additive effect of attention into goal-relevant information.
source: Our empirical confidence data therefore provide further support to a multiplicative (Smith and Krajbich, 2019) instead of additive effect of attention into goal-relevant information.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modeling results and experimental data.

claim: The goal sets, from the beginning of the task, the allocation of attention and influences first-order processes such as choice, but also second order process such as confidence.
source: Overall, these data speak in favour of a coding scheme in which the goal sets, from the beginning of the task, the allocation of attention and, by doing so, influences first-order processes such as choice, but also second order process such as confidence.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental and modeling results.

claim: There has been surprisingly little experimental work in which the behavioural goal has been directly manipulated as the key experimental variable for studying the relation between attention and value.
source: Nevertheless, there has been a surprisingly little amount of experimental work in which the behavioural goal has been directly manipulated as the key experimental variable for studying the relation between attention and value.
evidence: This is a characterization of the state of the field.

claim: Frömer et al., 2019 found that behaviour and neural activity in the 'value network' was determined by goal-congruency and did not simply reflected the expected reward.
source: In the first study (Frömer et al., 2019), participants were shown a set of four items and asked, in half of the trials, to determine the best item and, in the second half, the worst item. In line with our findings, they found that behaviour and neural activity in the 'value network', including vmPFC and striatum, was determined by goal-congruency and did not simply reflected the expected reward.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited study.

claim: Kovach et al., 2014 found that the overall pattern of attention was mostly allocated according to the task goal.
source: In the second study, Kovach et al., 2014 implemented a design similar to our value-based experiment in which participants were required to indicate the item to keep and the one to discard. They found, similarly to our findings in the value-based experiment, that the overall pattern of attention was mostly allocated according to the task goal.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited study.

claim: Kovach et al., 2014 found that in the first few hundred milliseconds, attention was directed more prominently to the most valuable item in both conditions.
source: However, in the first few hundred milliseconds, these authors found that attention was directed more prominently to the most valuable item in both conditions.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited study.

claim: The current study did not replicate the finding that fixations were directed to the most valuable item in the early moments of the trial.
source: We did not replicate this last finding in our experiment (see Figure 3C and D and Appendix 2—figure 2, showing that fixations were randomly allocated during the early moments of the trial).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and D and Appendix 2—figure 2.

claim: The gaze-contingent presentation in the current study might have prevented an initial bottom-up attention grab from the most valuable item.
source: One possible reason for this discrepancy is that the experiment by Kovach and colleagues presented both items on the screen at the beginning of the task – unlike in our task, in which the item was presented in a gaze-contingent way (to avoid processing in the visual periphery). This setting might have triggered an initial and transitory bottom-up attention grab from the most valuable (and often most salient) item before the accumulation process started.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the difference between studies.

claim: When the agent needs to select the best item in a set, it is best to search for evidence that it is more likely to affect the top of the ranking.
source: When the agent needs to select the best item in a set, it is best to search for evidence that it is more likely to affect the top of the ranking (e.g. is the best item still the best one?); information that changes the middle or the bottom of the ranking is instead less valuable (e.g. is the item ranked as seven is now ranked as six?) because it would not affect the behavioural output.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the economic model.

claim: When choosing which item to discard, the optimal strategy involves acquiring information most informative of the bottom of the ranking and not the top.
source: When choosing which item to discard, instead, the optimal strategy involves acquiring information most informative of the bottom of the ranking and not the top.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the economic model.

claim: Context and behavioural demand have a powerful effect on how information is accumulated and processed.
source: The most far reaching conclusion of our work is that context and behavioural demand have a powerful effect on how information is accumulated and processed.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: This is a general effect that spans both more complex value-based choice and simpler perceptual choice.
source: Notably, our data show that this is a general effect that spans both more complex value-based choice and simpler perceptual choice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing results across the two experiments.

claim: Humans have developed a mechanism that prioritises the processing or recollection of the information that is most relevant for the behavioural response that is required.
source: Our conclusion is that, given the limited computational resources of the brain, humans have developed a mechanism that prioritises the processing or recollection of the information that is most relevant for the behavioural response that is required.
evidence: This is the main theoretical conclusion of the study.

claim: From the very beginning of the deliberation process, the context affects which information is processed, recalled, or attended to, with effects that spread into post-decision processing such as confidence estimation.
source: As we have shown here, from the very beginning of the deliberation process, the context — even when it is simple (like/dislike, most/fewest) or irrelevant from the experimenter perspective — affects which information is processed, recalled, or attended to, with effects that spread into post-decision processing such as confidence estimation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Many of the so-called 'biases' might be shown in a new light, given that participants are dealing with very different choices once the behavioural goal changes.
source: With this shift of perspective, it may well be the case that many of the so-called 'biases' will be shown in a new light, given that participants are dealing with very different choices once the behavioural goal changes.
evidence: This is a speculative implication of the findings.

claim: Evolution has equipped humans well to deal with ever-changing environments in the face of limited computational resources.
source: This viewpoint might provide a more encouraging picture of the human mind, by suggesting that evolution has equipped us well to deal with ever-changing environments in the face of limited computational resources.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Participants were asked to fast for 4 hr previous to the experiment, expecting they would be hungry and willing to spend money to buy a snack.
source: Participants were asked to fast for 4 hr previous to the experiment, expecting they would be hungry and willing to spend money to buy a snack.
evidence: This describes a methodological detail of the experiment.

claim: Pairs were selected using the value ratings given in the bidding task: using a median split, each item was categorised as high- or low-value for the agent.
source: Pairs were selected using the value ratings given in the bidding task: using a median split, each item was categorised as high- or low-value for the agent; these were then combined to produce 15 high-value, 15 low-value, and 30 mixed pairs, for a total of 60 pairs tailored to the participant's preferences.
evidence: This describes a methodological detail of the experiment.

claim: Participants' eye movements were recorded throughout the choice task and the presentation of food items was gaze-contingent.
source: Participants' eye movements were recorded throughout the choice task and the presentation of food items was gaze-contingent: participants could only see one item at a time depending on which box they looked at; following Folke et al., 2017, this was done to reduce the risk that participant, while gazing one item, would still look at the other item in their visual periphery.
evidence: This describes a methodological detail of the experiment.

claim: Forty volunteers gave their informed consent to take part in the Value Experiment research.
source: Forty volunteers gave their informed consent to take part in this research.
evidence: This describes the participant recruitment for the study.

claim: Thirty-one participants passed the exclusion criteria and were included in the analysis of the Value Experiment.
source: Of these, 31 passed the exclusion criteria and were included in the analysis (16 females, 17 males, aged 20–54, mean age of 28.8).
evidence: This describes the final sample for the Value Experiment.

claim: Forty volunteers were recruited for the Perceptual Experiment.
source: Forty volunteers were recruited for the second experiment.
evidence: This describes the participant recruitment for the Perceptual Experiment.

claim: Thirty-two participants were included in the behavioural and regression analyses of the Perceptual Experiment.
source: Thirty-two participants (22 females, 10 males, aged 19–50, mean age of 26.03) were included in the behavioural and regression analyses.
evidence: This describes the final sample for the Perceptual Experiment.

claim: The optimal strategy when choosing the best option is to acquire one more signal about item i1 or i2.
source: Proposition 1. The optimal strategy when choosing the best option is to acquire one more signal about item i1 or i2, that is, either the item with the currently highest expected value or the one with second highest value.
evidence: This is a formal proposition from the economic model.
